phonemes.desc: Velar nasal [ŋ] followed by open central vowel [a]. The initial ŋ is the same sound as English 'ng' in 'sing'; in Kunwinjku it is a regular word-initial consonant.
Palatal lateral approximant [ʎ], sometimes heard as a light 'ly' cluster; the tongue touches the hard palate and releases along the sides.
Mid back rounded vowel [ɔ] plus alveolar stop [d]. The final syllable is short and firm.

pronunciation.approximation: 'NGAL-yod' — start with the 'ng' of 'sing' followed by 'al', then a light 'yod' rhyming roughly with 'yod' in Hebrew scholarship.

pronunciation.note: The restoration capitalizes the initial N as a proper name, but the ASCII form *ngalyod* is otherwise identical. Because the distinctive phoneme ŋ is not representable in the basic ASCII set and because the name preserves no further diacritic or special letter, PuniCodex places the restored form **Ngalyod** in Tier 2: the capitalization signals scholarly citation form, while the underlying phonemic content remains the same. The plain ASCII form is a DNS compromise, not a misspelling.

domains.title: The Rainbow Serpent
domains.subtitle: Water, Law, Monsoon, and the Dreaming
domains.lead: Ngalyod is the great Rainbow Serpent of the Kunwinjku-speaking peoples of western Arnhem Land. In the wet season she — or he, for gender shifts with country and ceremony — arcs across the sky as the rainbow; in the dry she sleeps beneath the earth in waterholes, springs, and rocky escarpments. She is not merely a weather spirit: she is a creator being who carved out the rivers, stocked them with fish and waterlilies, and laid down the law that still governs the relationship between people, country, and kin.

cards.name: The Rainbow
cards.desc: Ngalyod is the rainbow itself, the visible sign of the serpent moving between waterholes and bringing the rains that renew the land.

cards.name: Waterhole Guardian
cards.desc: In the dry season Ngalyod rests in permanent waterholes; to disturb or pollute those places is to risk the serpent's anger.

cards.name: Law Giver
cards.desc: The Rainbow Serpent established moiety, marriage rules, and the ceremonial obligations that bind clans to country.

cards.name: Creator of Abundance
cards.desc: Ngalyod created the fish, waterlilies, and other foods of the wetlands; her body shaped the country people still live from.

mythology.lead: Ngalyod's stories are told in rock art galleries, song cycles, and ceremonial narratives across western Arnhem Land. The serpent is not a single fixed character but a continuum of powers: creator, law-giver, healer, and avenger. The myths explain why certain waterholes never dry, why the wet season returns, and why human beings must respect the boundaries between clans and countries.

myths.title: Carving the Country
myths.text: In the Dreaming, Ngalyod travelled across a flat and featureless land. Where she raised her body, ridges and escarpments rose; where she lay down, waterholes and rivers formed. Her tracks are the deep channels that still carry floodwater in the wet. Every permanent waterhole is remembered as a place where the serpent paused, and each is owned and cared for by the clan whose ancestors witnessed her passage.

myths.title: The Two Moieties
myths.text: Ngalyod divided the people into moieties, the two halves of society whose rules of marriage, ceremony, and land ownership still structure Kunwinjku social life. The serpent's law is not written down; it is sung, painted, and enacted in ceremony. To break it is to disturb the balance of country and to invite illness, accident, or the withdrawal of the waters.

myths.title: The Wet's Return
myths.text: When the first storms build over the Arnhem Land plateau, elders say that Ngalyod is moving from one waterhole to another. The rainbow is her body seen between earth and sky; the thunder is her voice. The arrival of the wet season is therefore not only a meteorological event but a ceremonial one, requiring the songs and restrictions that announce the serpent's presence.

myths.title: The Boy who Laughed
myths.text: A widely recorded story tells of a boy who mocked or wounded Ngalyod. In retaliation the serpent swallowed him and carried him underground through the water system, eventually releasing him far from his own country — or, in some versions, transforming him into a landmark. The tale teaches that the sacred must be approached with restraint, and that waterholes are not ordinary places.

etymology.derivation: The name is attested in Kunwinjku and closely related Gunwingguan languages as the term for the rainbow and for the great serpent identified with it. No deeper external etymology has been securely established; the word belongs to the Indigenous language ecology of western Arnhem Land.

syncretism: The Rainbow Serpent is one of the most widely distributed figures in Aboriginal Australia, yet it is not a single deity under many names. Each language group knows a distinct serpent with its own country, kinship, and ceremonies: Yurlungur in Yolŋu country, Wagyl in Noongar country, Julunggul among some north-eastern groups, and Ngalyod among the Kunwinjku. Anthropologists and art historians have long debated whether these figures share a common origin or whether the rainbow-serpent concept is a convergence of regional powers onto a similar natural sign. What is clear is that Ngalyod must be understood on Kunwinjku terms first, before any wider comparison is attempted.
culturalLegacy: Ngalyod survives most visibly in the x-ray rock art of western Arnhem Land, where the serpent is painted with internal organs, ribs, and backbone showing — a visual convention that identifies the figure as both animal and ancestor. These galleries, some thousands of years old, are now part of a living heritage managed by traditional owners in partnership with archaeologists and park authorities. In contemporary Australia the Rainbow Serpent has also become a national symbol of Indigenous ecological knowledge, appearing in public art, children's books, and environmental education. That wider fame brings a risk: the specific clan-owned meanings of Ngalyod can be flattened into a generic 'Aboriginal' icon. The restoration of the Kunwinjku name is a small act of precision against that flattening.
extendedMeditation:
Ngalyod is not a god in the sense of a being who stands outside the world and rules it. She is country itself in serpent form: the water that does not forget, the law that does not sleep, the rainbow that returns after every drought. To speak her name is to acknowledge that the land is not inert backdrop but a living body with memory.

The name also asks something of the people who use it. In a colonial country where many Aboriginal languages were suppressed, to restore Ngalyod rather than settle for the generic English 'Rainbow Serpent' is to recognise a specific intellectual tradition. The ASCII form *ngalyod* keeps the letters but loses the capital that marks a proper name; more importantly, it loses the social fact that the name belongs to a language and a people. Unicode cannot carry the whole of that inheritance, but it can at least make the name visible as a name.
originalScriptNote: The Kunwinjku languages were traditionally oral; no Indigenous writing system was used before European contact. The form Ngalyod is therefore a modern scholarly transliteration designed to represent the spoken name in the Latin alphabet. The initial capital marks it as a proper noun, and the digraph ng represents the single velar nasal phoneme /ŋ/. Because the name is not Greek, Devanagari, or CJK, the project labels it 'Scholarly Transliteration' rather than 'Original Script'.

archaeology: The primary material witnesses to Ngalyod are the rock-art galleries of western Arnhem Land, notably at sites such as Ubirr, Nourlangie, and the Arnhem Land plateau, where Rainbow Serpent figures appear in both naturalistic and x-ray styles across millennia of painting. Excavated occupation deposits, stone tool scatters, and fish-trap complexes document the long-term human use of the waterholes and wetlands associated with the serpent. These places remain under the custodianship of their traditional-owner clans; access and reproduction of designs are regulated by Indigenous cultural authority.
